items.title: Virginia Mayhew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2022
items.q: that was when Wynton Marsalis and all the young lions came out and it was sort of like — when he came out it was sort of the people at the New School, the teachers and stuff referred to him sort of like the jazz police.

ctx.x: What changed in the New York scene from the time you arrived like and the next fifteen or twenty years?

Well the New York scene, I mean there are a lot of different scenes. So you know there’s the free scene, and if you’re just talking about jazz okay, but then there are all the other things like salsa and everything, but in jazz there’s the free scene and I played with this group called the Twelve Tone Funk Orchestra when I first got there, it was so much fun. But the straight ahead, you know the predominant jazz scene was basically a bebop scene. And that was when Wynton Marsalis and all the young lions came out…

would regret later and I probably will but I’m going to say it again now and I said there’s this thing happening — in 1998 — so that was a little over ten years after I moved there. I call it “Brooklyn White Boy” jazz. And it’s exactly what it has become, you know, the end of swing and blues and digging in and that would be — I know I’m a nasty person but that is the biggest change is like the standard when I moved here in ’87 was bebop was the standard.
